title: Separating Common and Unique Directions for Model Merging
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Task-level components are highly heterogeneous: most directions have low cross-task dispersion, while a small high-dispersion tail holds disproportionate energy.
layout: 4 panels in a row, histogram then decile bar pair per model, insets and annotations
description: A single row of four small plots comparing two models. Panels (a) and (c) are teal histograms of per-direction dispersion D_k = std_i(Σ_ik) for Llama and ViT. Each is sharply peaked near zero with a long thin right tail, plus a shaded inset zooming into the tail (labelled 'Tail: 93'). Panels (b) and (d) are bar charts of energy share across dispersion deciles from 0-10 to 90-100. The first nine bars are short and pale yellow, and the last bar is tall and dark orange. An orange arrow and text call out 'Top 10%: 53%' for Llama and 'Top 10%: 77%' for ViT. A dashed gray line marks the uniform share. The eye goes first to the orange top-decile bars and labels.
caption: Direction-level heterogeneity in task vectors. Motivating examples from representative matrix layers of Llama-3.2-3B (mlp.gate\_proj) and ViT-B/16 (mlp.c\_proj). (a,\,c) Distribution of cross-task dispersion scores over shared directions. (b,\,d) Share of total directional energy in each dispersion-ranked decile.
abstract: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models without additional training, and arithmetic methods have emerged as a simple yet effective way to merge models without data. However, existing arithmetic methods treat task vectors in parameter space and apply a single element-wise rule to directions that can differ in mergeability. In a shared directional basis, we find a consistent two-regime structure: a low-dispersion common bulk shared across tasks and a high-dispersion task-dominated tail that carries disproportionate energy. These findings motivate Common--Unique Subspace Decomposition (CUSD), a data-free pre-merging method that separates task vectors into common and unique directional components, merges the common components with a downstream arithmetic operator, and retains unique residuals separately. Experiments across $11$ base models, four model families, and four arithmetic-based merging operators show that CUSD improves 42 of 44 model--operator combinations and achieves up to 22.5% improvement over the corresponding baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/stwang666/CUSD
